book.title: When: The Scientific Secrets of Perfect Timing
book.author: Daniel H. Pink

confidence_note: The reference TR text builds on Ernest Hemingway's morning writing routine and says Pink 'reviewed thousands of studies' and found Hemingway 'instinctively right'; the Hemingway framing and that claim cannot be confidently attributed to When and are omitted. The book's own evidence for the daily pattern is used instead: the Twitter mood study and the Wieth and Zacks insight-problem study. Pink's pattern (peak, trough, recovery) applies to most people but reverses for night owls; the reference text's claim of a fixed morning peak for everyone is corrected. Chronotype percentages are omitted.
facts: Pink describes a study of hundreds of millions of tweets from many countries in which positive mood rose in the morning, dipped in the afternoon and rose again in the evening.
He summarizes the day as peak, trough and recovery for most people; for night owls the order runs roughly in reverse.
During the peak, people are best at analytical work that needs focus and ignoring distractions.
In a study by Mareike Wieth and Rose Zacks, people solved insight problems better at their non-optimal time of day, when they were a little less focused and more open to unexpected connections.
Pink's advice: find your chronotype, then match task type to time, analytical work in the peak and insight work in the recovery, and avoid important work in the trough when possible.
tension: The same person can be sharp at 9 a.m. and a better creative thinker at 7 p.m., so 'when am I most productive?' has no single answer.
opening_idea: Begin with the tweets: millions of people across the world, without meaning to, left a record of their mood rising and falling at the same times of day.

lessons.idea: Timing affects different kinds of work differently.
lessons.anchor: Analytical tasks favored the peak; insight problems favored the off-peak.

lessons.idea: A slightly unfocused mind can see new connections.
lessons.anchor: Wieth and Zacks found insight improved when people were less alert.

lessons.idea: The daily pattern depends on chronotype.
lessons.anchor: Pink notes the peak-trough-recovery order roughly reverses for night owls.

reflect: When during the day do you do your most careful work, and is that by choice or by habit?
Have you had a good idea at a time you weren't trying to work?
reflect_final: Tomorrow, move one analytical task into your peak and one open-ended problem into your recovery period, then compare how each went.

use_cases.situation: Scheduling a budget review and a brainstorm in the same week.
use_cases.move: Put the budget review in the morning and, citing Pink's insight-problem study, suggest the brainstorm late afternoon.

use_cases.situation: A friend who's a night owl apologizes for late messages about work.
use_cases.move: Tell them Pink says owls' peak runs later, and ask when their clearest thinking actually happens.
Block your first two focused hours for your hardest analytical task this week, and notice if afternoons suit other work.

pocket_idea: Pink's tweet data show a daily mood curve most of us share, and the insight study shows the dip isn't only wasted: the slightly foggy hours suit different work.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: People solved creative puzzles better when they were slightly tired, not at their sharpest.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Pink uses a massive tweet study to show mood peaks, dips and recovers daily; then an insight study shows that the off-peak hours actually help creative problem solving.
conversation_variants.question_idea: When in the day does your best idea usually show up?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: From 'find your most productive hour' to 'find the right hour for each kind of work.'
